name: RPG
description: Character growth, items and a world with quests to follow. Systems-heavy, so the stats, inventory and save code each get a Tech doc.

pillars.name: My Character, My Way
pillars.feeling: the build is mine and it shows

pillars.name: Choices With Weight
pillars.rulesOut: choices that lead to the same outcome

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A party-based fantasy RPG where the player builds a character their way and shapes the fate of a fractured kingdom.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Take a quest.
2. Explore a region and fight what's in it.
3. Earn experience and loot.
4. Level up, change gear, and pick the next quest.

gameExamples.heading: Non-goals
gameExamples.text:
- Multiplayer.
- Real-time twitch combat.
- Crafting as a main activity.

docs.title: Character
docs.summary: Who the player is and how they grow.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can create a character and choose their look and class.
- As a player, I can see my character's stats and gear.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A character screen with stats, gear and abilities.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text: - Appearance can be changed later; class can't.

docs.title: Progression
docs.summary: Experience, leveling and the pacing of power growth.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can gain experience and level up.
- As a player, I can choose how to spend skill points.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - An experience bar and a level-up moment.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Leveling slows down after the main story's level range.
- Points can be refunded for a cost.

docs.title: Classes and Abilities
docs.summary: Classes, skills and ability trees that define how characters play.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can pick a class with its own playstyle.
- As a player, I can unlock and upgrade abilities in a tree.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - An ability tree with locked, available and learned abilities.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Each class has three ability branches.
- Abilities have cooldowns, not mana.

docs.title: Stats
docs.summary: Attributes and derived values, and how they feed into every other system.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Each character has base attributes; derived stats are calculated from attributes, gear and active effects whenever one changes.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UStatsComponent`: attributes, derived stats and modifiers
- `FStatModifier`: an additive or multiplicative change from gear or effects

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Attribute definitions and formulas in a data asset.
- Level curves in a curve table.

docs.title: Ability System
docs.summary: How abilities, cooldowns and effects are implemented.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Abilities are built on the Gameplay Ability System: each ability is a gameplay ability, effects change attributes, and tags block abilities from overlapping.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectAbilitySystemComponent`: on every character
- `UProjectGameplayAbility`: base class for abilities
- `UProjectAttributeSet`: health, mana and combat attributes

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Ability and effect assets per class.
- Gameplay tags for states and blocks.

docs.title: Character Models
docs.summary: Player and companion meshes, rigs, animations and customization parts.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Player body meshes | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Armor sets | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Hair and faces | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Combat animations | Animation | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Grounded fantasy: worn materials, muted colors, gear that shows its history.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Modular fantasy character packs on one skeleton.
- Armor sets that cover the same body parts.
- Animation packs for sword, bow and magic.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Sci-fi or modern clothing.
- Packs on different skeletons.
- Overly glossy materials.

docs.title: Combat
docs.summary: How fights play out: turns or real time, targeting, damage and status effects.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can attack, dodge and block with simple inputs.
- As a player, I can read what an enemy is about to do.
- As a player, I can feel each hit land.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Wind-up animations before enemy attacks.
- Hit flashes, sounds and a short pause on impact.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every enemy attack can be avoided.
- Damage numbers stay small enough to reason about.

docs.title: Combat Code
docs.summary: Turn order or real-time loop, damage calculation and status effects.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Attacks spawn hitboxes for a few frames; overlaps send damage events to anything with a health component. Status effects are applied as timed modifiers.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UCombatComponent`: starts attacks and spawns hitboxes
- `UHealthComponent`: takes damage, fires death events
- `UStatusEffect`: a timed modifier (burn, slow, stun)

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Attack data (damage, frames, hitbox size) in data assets.
- Status effects in a DataTable.

docs.title: Combat Effects
docs.summary: Spell and hit VFX, combat sounds and animations.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hit sparks | VFX | Placeholder | To source |
| Impact sounds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Camera shakes | Data | Placeholder | To source |
| Death effects | VFX | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Short, bright and readable: effects confirm a hit without hiding the next threat.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Niagara VFX packs with hits, slashes and explosions.
- Impact sound libraries with light, medium and heavy variations.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Long-lasting particles that clutter the screen.
- Effects in a different style from the characters.

docs.title: Items
docs.summary: Everything the player can own, carry and use, and where it comes from.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can pick up, equip and use items.
- As a player, I can compare an item with what I have.
- As a player, I can drop or sell items I don't need.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Item rarity shown by color.
- Stat comparisons when hovering an item.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Inventory has a weight or slot limit.
- Quest items can't be dropped.

docs.title: Equipment
docs.summary: Gear slots and how equipment changes the character.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can equip weapons, armor and accessories.
- As a player, I can see how gear changes my stats.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Gear visible on the character.
- Green and red stat changes when comparing.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- One item per slot.
- Some gear needs a minimum level.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.summary: How items are stored, sorted and limited, and the item data format.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: An inventory component holds item instances in slots; item definitions are data assets, and instances store only what changes (count, durability).

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UInventoryComponent`: slots, add, remove and move
- `UItemDefinition`: data asset per item
- `FItemInstance`: count, durability and rolls

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Item definitions as data assets.
- Inventory saved as a list of item instances.

docs.title: Item Assets
docs.summary: Item meshes, icons and the item data tables.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Item meshes | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Item icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Item data | Data | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Items read clearly at icon size; rarity is shown through color and glow, not detail.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Item packs that include both meshes and matching icons.
- Icon packs with a consistent background and lighting.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Icons rendered with different camera angles.
- Mixing realistic and cartoon items.

docs.title: Quests
docs.summary: The story and the tasks that move the player through it.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can accept quests from characters.
- As a player, I can track several quests at once.
- As a player, I can see where to go next.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A journal with active and completed quests.
- Map markers for tracked objectives.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Main quests can't be abandoned.
- Side quests can be done in any order.

docs.title: Dialogue
docs.summary: Conversations and choices, and how the player sees them.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can talk to characters and choose what to say.
- As a player, I can see who's speaking.
- As a player, I can review what was said.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Subtitles with the speaker's name.
- Choices that hint at their tone.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Important choices can't be skipped.
- Dialogue can be advanced but never auto-skips choices.

docs.title: Quest System
docs.summary: Quest states, objectives, triggers and the journal.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Quests are data assets with ordered objectives. Objectives listen for gameplay events (kill, collect, talk) and advance when their conditions are met.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UQuestSubsystem`: active quests and their states
- `UQuestDefinition`: data asset with objectives and rewards
- `UQuestObjective`: listens for one kind of event

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Quest definitions as data assets.
- Quest states saved per quest.

docs.title: Story Assets
docs.summary: Dialogue scripts, voice lines and cutscenes.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dialogue scripts | Data | Placeholder | To source |
| Voice lines | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Cutscenes | Animation | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Dialogue is warm and grounded; voices match the characters' ages and backgrounds.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Voice actors with a range of character voices.
- Cinematic animation packs for conversations.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Modern slang in a fantasy setting.
- Text-to-speech placeholders shipping in the final game.

docs.title: World
docs.summary: The places the player explores and who lives there.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can explore distinct regions.
- As a player, I can find my way back to places I've been.
- As a player, I can notice that the world reacts to what I've done.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Each region has its own look and landmarks.
- A map that fills in as I explore.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Regions open up as the story progresses.
- Fast travel only between places I've visited.

docs.title: NPCs
docs.summary: Non-player characters: schedules, roles and interactions.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can talk to townsfolk.
- As a player, I can trade with merchants.
- As a player, I can notice NPCs going about their day.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - NPCs with names and roles shown on hover.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- NPCs follow daily schedules.
- Important NPCs can't be killed.

docs.title: Regions
docs.summary: Environment kits, props and landscapes for each region.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forest kit | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Town kit | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Landscape materials | Material | Placeholder | To source |
| Foliage | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Each region has its own palette and landmark shapes, on a shared grounded-fantasy material base.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Fantasy environment packs with towns, forests and ruins.
- Foliage packs that work with the engine's foliage tools.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Stylized cartoon packs.
- Regions so similar the player can't tell them apart.

docs.title: Economy
docs.summary: Currencies, shops and crafting, and how they balance.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can earn gold from quests and loot.
- As a player, I can spend it on gear and services.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Gold always visible in menus.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Prices scale with the region.
- Selling returns a quarter of an item's value.

docs.title: Shops
docs.summary: Vendors, prices and buy-back rules.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can buy and sell items at shops.
- As a player, I can buy back something I sold by mistake.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A shop screen with my inventory beside the shop's.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Shops restock daily.
- Buy-back keeps the last ten sold items.

docs.title: Crafting
docs.summary: Turning materials into items: recipes and stations.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can combine materials into items.
- As a player, I can see which recipes I can make right now.
- As a player, I can queue several crafts.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A recipe list with missing materials highlighted.
- A progress bar for each craft.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Some recipes need a station.
- Crafting can't be cancelled after it finishes.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.title: UI Art
docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Fonts (headings, body) | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Panel and button skins | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Input prompt icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.

docs.title: Save and Load
docs.summary: What persists between sessions, how it's stored, and how saves stay compatible.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A save game object holds everything that persists. Systems register what they need saved; saving serializes it to a slot, loading restores it before the level starts. Saves carry a version number so old saves can be migrated.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USaveSubsystem`: saves and loads slots, runs migrations
- `UProjectSaveGame`: the saved data, with a version field
- `ISaveable`: interface for systems that write and read their part

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Save slots in the platform's save location.
- A version number per save, bumped on every breaking change.
